zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Lexical aid consulted after independent scan reading: Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510, supplied page subset, CC BY 4.0. [Dataset](https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html); [license](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). The scan remains authoritative for letters, typeface, marks, spacing and line division.

runs.text: que não ſaya o vento, quando apertão os folles.

lines.note: Completes the leather-valve definition from f358: air must not escape when the bellows are compressed. The scan reads não and folles, correcting nũo and feles; the doubled l in folles is preserved.

Necobuqi is referred to the preferred Necogaqi by Meliùs, then defined as a mat. The headword's o and the l in Meliùs correct OCR u and r; damaged letters remain guided by the visible repeated mat term below.
The mat is of tightly worked cord or straw. Muito tapada refers to its close texture and completes the preceding description.

runs.text: Certa esteira großa feita de corda,

lines.note: Necogaqi is a thick mat made from cord or straw. The initial syllable is Ne-, correcting OCR Na-, and matches the cross-reference two rows above.

runs.text: ou palha ſobre que poem arroz, trigo, &c.

lines.note: Rice, wheat, and similar grain are placed on this mat. The sentence describes its use rather than adding further materials from which it is made.
Necogui is uprooting. Arrancar corrects OCR urrancar; Qiuo begins the example with trees as the object.
Qiuo necoguini ſuru means pulling trees out by the roots. The Portuguese translation continues with the root on the next row.
Raiz juntamente specifies removal together with the root. The surviving descender supports initial j in juntamente, restoring the letter lost by OCR.

runs.text: Lauores abertos, que ha em algũs a

lines.note: Necoma denotes openwork decoration on a fan. The Portuguese reads Lauores rather than Lauoros; a at the right edge begins abanos below without a supplied hyphen.

runs.text: banos nas caninhas de fora que ſão hum pouco-

lines.note: The openwork is in the outer bamboo strips of certain fans. The scan does print a terminal hyphen after pouco although mais is a separate word on the next row; preserve this printing anomaly.
The outer strips are somewhat wider. This completes pouco mais largas and explains where the openwork is made.
Necqi means fever. Necqiga ſaſu introduces the onset of fever, with Apon continued on the next row; no hyphen is added where none is securely printed.
Tar completes apontar, the beginning or arrival of fever. Necqiga ſamuru then introduces the fever subsiding.
Irſe or deſpedirſe a febre translates the fever departing. The same fever entry continues across all three physical rows.
Necquai is explained by Ayaxime ſaguru and glossed as doubting something. The Japanese wording is preserved rather than replaced with a modern equivalent inferred from the Portuguese.
Gũa completes algũa and closes the doubt definition. The tilde remains unexpanded on the divided word.

runs.text: Paos que atraueſão na caſa entre colũ-

lines.note: Neda denotes timbers crossing between house posts below the floor. The line-end sequence is colũ-, not OCR colũi-; the apparent extra i belongs to the worn final minims of the abbreviated form.

runs.text: na, & columna por de baixo do ſolhado: no Xi-

lines.note: Na completes colũna; the second occurrence is printed in full as columna. The regional term Ximo begins after no and is divided after Xi-, within the Portuguese explanation.
Mo completes Ximo, followed by the regional equivalent Vôdoco. The circumflex is preserved; the Japanese equivalent is not treated as another independent headword.
Nedare describes being deceitful or underhanded. The Portuguese reads refolhado, with f rather than OCR long ſ, consistent with its repeated form below.
Nedareta fito is a deceitful person. The example repeats the headword's Ne-, correcting OCR Nadareta; refo- begins the divided Portuguese adjective.
Lhado completes refolhado, followed by dißimulado and trapaceiro. The scan supports continuous dißimulado rather than the OCR's internal split dißi mulado.
Nedocoro is a sleeping chamber. The concise Portuguese gloss is retained without expanding the Japanese compound in the transcription.
Nedoi describes a curious person who investigates things minutely. Miuda continues into mente on the next line without an added terminal hyphen.
This finishes miuda / mente from the preceding row and states that Nedoi examines any matter minutely and from its root. The initial mente belongs to the Portuguese adverb, not a new Japanese word.

Nefan denotes the death or nirvana of Shaka; the following Japanese Nefanni iru describes entering that state. Xaca is embedded in the Portuguese definition; the headword's historical f is retained rather than replaced by modern h.
This short indented gloss completes Nefanni iru: Shaka dies. Xaca is again a Japanese name inside Portuguese, and the whole row is printed in italic, not a separate entry.

Nefanguiǒ names the scripture associated with nirvana; the Portuguese calls it a book that Shaka explained in preaching. The final nasal contraction in prègãdo and the printed accents are retained; the lexical identification does not modernize the title.

Negai is the verb 'desire'; Goxǒuo ne- begins an example about desiring salvation or a favorable afterlife. The verb's contracted forms ǒ and ǒta are printed with their marks; the hyphen divides the example across the next row.
The opening gǒ completes negǒ from the previous row, followed by the gloss 'desire salvation.' The translation narrows the religious sense of Goxǒ in this example; gǒ is not an independent headword.
This separate nominal Negai is glossed simply 'desire,' in contrast to the conjugated verb above. The small final stop and the long s in Deſejo are retained.

Negauacuua introduces a wish: the Portuguese equivalents are 'would that' and 'may God grant.' The historical doubled uu and the spellings Oxala, prouuera and Deos are preserved rather than modernized.

runs.text: Rosto de quem dorme, ou dormio

lines.note: Negauo describes the face of someone asleep or recently awakened. The Portuguese relative clause continues into the next row; the Japanese au sequence belongs to the historical spelling of the face compound.
The brief ha pouco finishes 'slept a short time ago' from the preceding definition. Its indentation and terminal stop distinguish this continuation from the two following Negui headwords.

This Negui is a shrine functionary, described as a man who serves the kami. The Portuguese plural camis is the embedded Japanese religious term; the second Negui below has an unrelated vegetable sense.

The homonymous Negui here means onions, described as dry onions without leaves. The visible ſ forms in ſecas and ſem are retained, as is the distinction from the shrine-office entry immediately above.
Neguiri is bargaining over a price. The principal forms ru, itta show the verb's inflection, distinct from the different verbal gloss introduced by the paragraph sign on the next row.

Fitouo neguiru introduces the sense of glaring at someone; the Portuguese begins Reſgalar os o- and continues with 'eyes' below. The citation label X is retained; the unusual Reſgalar is not silently modernized to regalar.

runs.text: lhos a alguem como quem o reprehende.

lines.note: The opening lhos completes o-lhos, and the rest explains looking at someone as if reproaching them. The row remains a continuation of the example, not a new entry; the historical reprehende is preserved.

runs.text: Iunto da raiz da aruore, ou bambu.

lines.note: Neguiua means the area immediately at a tree's or bamboo's root. The scan separates da raiz, so the OCR's daraiz is divided; the headword's gui spelling is consistent with the voiced root-boundary compound.

Negoi and negoi fito describe a person who sleeps a great deal. The single printed long s in Peſoa is retained rather than expanded to the more usual double-s spelling; the final quantifier follows below.
The isolated muito completes 'a person who sleeps much.' Its shortness is genuine; the following Negoto starts a new entry and is not joined to this row.
Negoto is speech in dreams or sleep-talking. The Japanese example starts Negotouo and takes its verb on the next physical row; no additional punctuation or hyphen is inserted at the column edge.

The scan reads yǔ, completing 'speak in one's sleep'; the OCR's extra final i is removed because the apparent stroke is part of the accented u. The Portuguese explicitly glosses the complete preceding example.

runs.text: Fala, ou voz do que està acordado

lines.note: Negoye is the voice of someone recently awakened rather than the sleep-talk in the preceding entry. The Portuguese description continues below; the grave in està is retained.
This finishes the definition with 'a short time after sleep.' The initial ha belongs to the Portuguese time expression and is not a Japanese syllable or a new entry.

Negura denotes the place where birds sleep, a roost. The separate P label near the right edge is roman, not part of the italic definition. Enlargement shows no stop after P, unlike P. at the top of the next column, so the OCR-supplied final period is removed. The column ends after this complete entry.

Negutaregami denotes hair disordered by sleeping; the Portuguese reads ficão, with a visible c omitted by OCR, rather than fião. The separate P label is roman. The definition continues on the indented row below.
This completes 'badly arranged after sleeping' from Negutaregami. The scan places the row inward relative to the headword, so the missing indentation marker is restored; it is not another entry.

Negi, zzuru, ita is the verb 'twist,' both transitive and intransitive in the Portuguese gloss. The historical zzuru ending and the tilde over the u of algũa are retained rather than assimilated to modern nejiru.
After completing 'some thing,' Faxiraga negita illustrates a wooden pillar becoming twisted. The Japanese g in negita and the Portuguese Entortouſe are supported by the shape-change sense.

runs.text: ou torceoſe a columna de pao. ¶

lines.note: The first clause finishes the pillar example; Taqeuo then starts a second example whose verb follows below. The wooden-column gloss and the bamboo object must not be combined into one Japanese sentence.
Negiru completes Taqeuo negiru, explained as breaking bamboo by twisting it. The double o of torcendoo is visibly printed and represents the appended object pronoun, not OCR duplication.
Negiai describes grappling and twisting one another's arms. The two contracted forms bear carons; the final tor- divides the Portuguese infinitive across the next row.
This finishes tor-cerem os braços, 'twist the arms,' with &c. It is a short continuation of the reciprocal-action entry, not a Japanese compound or a new gloss.

Negicubi is a twisted neck; the paragraph sign begins the verbal expression Negicubi ſuru. The voiced gi in the headword is consistent with the neighboring twisting compounds and is left in the printed spelling.
The opening ſuru completes the Japanese expression 'twist the neck,' which the Portuguese translates directly. The long s is part of the roman Japanese verb, while the following gloss is italic.
Negifanaxi means pulling something off by twisting it. The visible f belongs to the historical hanashi element; the principal form ſu and aita are retained, and the alternative gloss continues below.
The phrase 'or detach' supplies the alternative explanation of Negifanaxi. The Portuguese deſapegar has a long s; the short continuation stays attached to the preceding verb entry.
Negigane is iron twisted like a screw. The compound combines the twisting element with metal; the Portuguese parafuſo confirms this rather than a cutting implement.
Negiguiri is a European auger or gimlet. The scan prints Europa as one word, so the spurious OCR space in Euro pa is removed; the historical Portuguese Verruma remains unchanged.

The damaged second letter of the headword retains the horizontal trace of e, giving Negimochi rather than Nagimochi. The gloss names a kind of mochi; Mochis is a Japanese food word embedded in the Portuguese sentence.

Negiqebito is equated with Neijin and described as a malicious person. The synonym after i is independent Japanese, not a Japanese term embedded within Portuguese; the further character trait continues below.

The continuation adds refolhado, 'devious' or 'dissembling.' Its f is visible and meaningful, agreeing with the other descriptions of deceitful people on this page rather than being a long-s spelling.
Negiqiri means severing or breaking by twisting. The printed abbreviated principal forms u, itta are retained, and the final que- belongs to the Portuguese quebrar on the next row.

After completing quebrar, the example begins Futçuto negiqitte nagueſute-: twisting off sharply and casting away. The scan supports gi in negiqitte and the long s in nagueſute; the terminal hyphen is visible.
The initial ta completes nagueſuteta; Xid. is the following citation label. The Portuguese says 'twisting with force and breaking,' with que- again divided at the right edge.
The opening brando completes quebrando, followed by 'threw away.' The printed arremeſou has one long s and is not modernized to arremessou; the row completes the previous example.

The headword is Negixibori, wringing out by twisting; a worn g had been read as punctuation in Ne,ixibori. Its lower curved remnant and the neighboring negi compounds support restoring the letter while retaining the printed forms u, otta.

Neijin, paraphrased Fetçurǒ fito, is a flattering and deceitful person. The Portuguese second adjective is split re- / falſado; the Japanese paraphrase is standalone and is not a typeface-toggle term.
The opening falſado completes refalſado, 'false' or 'deceitful.' Its initial f must be distinguished from the later long s in the same word; the row is a continuation of Neijin.

Neiri is falling asleep or being asleep. The scan leaves a visible gap after the capital A in A dormecer, so that unusual spacing is retained rather than silently joined; the Japanese forms remain u, itta.

runs.text: Sono profundo de hum que começa

lines.note: The headword reads Neiribana, with i rather than the OCR's a after Ne; the repeated example below supplies a useful same-page comparator. The gloss describes the deep sleep of someone just beginning to sleep.

After completing the definition, Neiribana gia fodoni, voco- begins 'because this is the first deep sleep, do not wake [the sleeper].' The final hyphen divides the negative command across the next row.

runs.text: Por que està na força, ou meo do ſo-

lines.note: The initial ſuna completes vocoſuna, the command not to wake someone. The Portuguese describes being in the strength or middle of sleep, with ſo- divided at the right edge; the grave in està is preserved.
This completes ſono and the prohibition 'do not wake [the sleeper].' The historical eſperteis is printed without an initial d and is retained, rather than changed to modern desperteis.
Neixa is a flatterer who deceives with fair words. The Portuguese pala- continues on the next line; this belongs with the subsequent moral-character entries, not the earlier sleeping vocabulary.
The opening uras completes palauras, and the adverb reads dißimuladamente, with a worn but visible a where OCR supplied u. It explains deception by dissimulation; the printed ß ligature is retained.

runs.text: Coração de homem desta laya refalſa-

lines.note: This Neixin refers to the heart or disposition of a deceitful person. The second adjective divides refalſa- / do; the gloss distinguishes this entry from the homonymous servant entry two rows below.
The brief do, &c. finishes refalſado from the preceding row. No headword or extra word is missing here; it is simply the end of the character-description gloss.

The second Neixin denotes a flattering, treacherous servant. The printed gloss distinguishes the servant sense from the preceding heart/disposition sense without requiring different spelling of the Japanese headword.

runs.text: Rabaças que tem a raiz comprida.

lines.note: Nejeri is a long-rooted kind of herb, explained by Portuguese Rabaças. The central letters of the headword are abraded, but the visible traces support the supplied Nejeri; the text is not normalized to modern seri spelling.

runs.text: Fortaleza principal onde reſide o ca

lines.note: Nejiro is the principal fortress where the commander resides. The scan supports the narrow i in reſide, omitted by OCR; the final ca is completed as capitão on the next row, without a clearly printed terminal hyphen.
The opening pitão completes ca-pitão from the fortress definition. The tilde belongs over a in the printed ending; the row is only the end of the Portuguese noun, not an independent Japanese entry.
Nemari is being silent without saying anything. The principal forms u, atta and the long s in Eſtar and ſem are retained; further examples and another sense follow below.

Nematta fito and nemarimono are alternative Japanese descriptions of the silent person. The Portuguese Ho- starts Homem on the next row; the alternatives are standalone Japanese and not embedded typeface terms.
The first clause completes 'a silent and shrewd man'; the paragraph sign introduces another sense of Nemari, concerning food beginning to spoil. The final Come- continues directly into the next row.

runs.text: çarſe a danar, ou eſtar ſentido o peixe, &c.

lines.note: The initial çarſe completes Começarſe, and the visible cedilla corrects the OCR's plain c. The gloss describes fish and similar food beginning to go bad or being affected, a distinct sense from remaining silent.

The Japanese example lists fish, mochi and cooked rice as things that spoil. The printed stop after mochi is retained even though a modern list would normally use commas; this is a standalone example, not a Portuguese sentence.

The Portuguese gloss translates the example as fish, mochi and so forth going bad. Here Mochis, unlike mochi in the preceding Japanese example, is embedded within Portuguese and is flagged for optional whole-word typeface review.

Nemidaregami denotes loose, disordered hair after sleep, close in meaning to the column's opening entry. The Portuguese Cabellos here has doubled l, unlike Cabelos above, and the nasal contraction in deſcõcer- is preserved.
This completes deſcõcer-tados and specifies 'after sleeping.' The scan supports the separated de pois, which is retained rather than normalized to depois elsewhere on the page.

runs.text: Certa laya de peças brancas de Iapão.

lines.note: Nemonji names a kind of white Japanese cloth or cloth pieces. The Portuguese reads peças, and Iapão is the historical spelling in the definition; the register restriction follows on the last body row.

The entry ends with the label 'a word of women.' The scan's worn r belongs within Palaura, so the OCR space in Palaur a is removed. The lower-right Nemo. is a separate catchword and is not appended to this body line.
